query: In high-entropy alloys, what governs superconducting behavior and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, identify a controlled comparison against a baseline that could reveal the governing cause, predict the relative observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, define its boundary conditions, state what prior evidence would make it plausible, and specify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The high configurational entropy at the RE site in high-entropy alloy (HEA) superconductors enhances the superconducting properties by suppressing the planar disorder of the adjacent conducting layer.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy superconductors with a layered structure, specifically REOBiS2 with a high-entropy REO blocking layer.
generation.intervention: Substitution of various rare-earth elements at the RE site to create a high-entropy effect.
generation.conditions: Low temperatures, high pressures, and magnetic fields.
generation.structural_mediator: The layered structure of the HEA superconductor, with the high-entropy REO blocking layer and the superconducting BiS2 layer.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy at the RE site suppresses the planar disorder of the adjacent conducting layer, leading to enhanced superconducting properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved superconducting properties, such as higher critical temperatures and enhanced robustness against external perturbations.
generation.baseline: Conventional superconductors without the high-entropy effect.
generation.boundary: The high-entropy effect is limited to the RE site, and the superconducting properties are sensitive to the specific rare-earth elements used.
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between the high configurational entropy and the superconducting properties is not fully understood, and further research is needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the superconducting properties of HEA superconductors with varying levels of configurational entropy at the RE site.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the superconducting properties do not improve with increasing configurational entropy, the hypothesis is falsified.

In this framework, HEA superconductors represent one of the hot topics owing to the reported enhancement of superconducting properties , and the outstanding robustness of the superconducting phase against extremely high pressures, , magnetic fields, , and irradiation. , Among them, layered HEA superconductors have the significant advantage of having the high-entropy layers separately stacked with the superconducting layers, limiting the direct effect of disorder on the superconducting state. BiS2-based layered superconductors are a good example of such systems, given the remarkable correlation between structural and electronic properties prompted by a peculiar instability of the BiS2 lattice hosting the superconductivity − and by the local configuration of the overlying REO layer (Figure ). Furthermore, the structural and electronic behavior of the BiS2 superconducting layer is largely affected by an intrinsic in-plane atomic disorder, as it has been revealed by means of experimental probes sensitive to the local structure. −

In undoped REOBiS2 superconductors, the RE site determines the superconducting transition temperature. The RE site of REOBiS2 superconductors can be substituted for various RE elements, such as La/Ce, Ce/Nd, and Ce/Pr. Indeed, superconductivity can also be achieved by exploiting valence fluctuation at the RE site, as already reported for self-doped CeOBiS2 and EuFBiS2 superconductors. − Recently, several BiS2-based superconductors have been synthesized with a HEA-type REO blocking layer, where the RE site is randomly occupied by several rare-earth species. By investigating the high-entropy effects in the optimally doped REO0.5F0.5BiS2 compounds, a clear relation between the increasing configurational entropy at the RE site and the reported improvements of the superconducting properties emerges, associated with a suppression of the planar disorder of the adjacent conducting layer. Nevertheless, extrinsic doping by substitution also affects the disorder. Therefore, self-doping is more appropriate to explore the effect of high entropy.

The HEA concept can be useful for developing new superconducting materials containing an HEA site and/or HEA-type layers. To start with, the HEA superconductor Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti, with a transition temperature of 7.3 K, was discovered. In addition, this high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressures up to 190 GPa. Later, the relationship between superconductivity and the high-entropy effect was investigated. RBa2Cu3O7−δ (R-123) high-Tc cuprate superconducting polycrystalline samples with the HEA concept in the R-site were investigated. In an analogous way, previous reports showed the synthesis and superconducting properties of RO0.5F0.5BiS2 polycrystalline samples with the HEA concept in the R-site for the improvement of superconducting properties., However, in polycrystalline samples, the intrinsic properties were masked by the impurities and grain boundaries. Especially, the anisotropic properties cannot be measured using polycrystalline samples.
